name: Lung'Ie
confidence_why: Agostinho and Hyman (2021), from instrumental fieldwork with five speakers, find no evidence of stress and analyse Lung'Ie as a privative high-tone language, and Maurer (2009, 2013) likewise treats it as a two-tone language, but Agostinho (2015, 2019) had earlier argued for free lexical stress alongside tone and Traill and Ferraz (1981) for a free pitch accent with one prominent syllable per word, so the type of system has been genuinely contested even though the latest and fullest study, by the former dissenter herself, settles it.
catalog_citation: Agostinho, Ana Lívia & Larry M. Hyman. 2021. Word Prosody in Lung'Ie: One System or Two? Probus 33(1): 57-93. doi:10.1515/prbs-2021-0002. Quoted from the UC eScholarship postprint (item qt0661t1jh, 38 pp.).
catalog_locator: Postprint §1 end (pp. 2-3); §4.1 'Nouns' (pp. 12-13); §5 'Discussion: Tone and Stress?' (p. 25 and pp. 29-30, fn. 42); §6 'Conclusion and Implications' (pp. 30-31).
catalog_quote: As will be seen, we conclude that Lung’Ie has a privative /H/ (high) tone system [...] without stress, similar to other culminative H tone systems such as Somali (Hyman 1981, see also Green and Morrison 2016; Le Gac 2003), but with the unusual stress-like property of weight-to-tone. [...] The H can be in any syllable, although there is some skewing because of Portuguese stress placement. [...] In CV.CV words, the tone pattern is synchronically unpredictable. In 68% of the nouns with a H, the H is on the penultimate syllable. Out of the 32% remaining, 23% have a final H and 9% have an antepenultimate H. [...] In our investigation, we did not find any evidence for stress in toneless words. [...] Regarding all-Ø words, we found no evidence of a prominent syllable, i. e., no phonetic correlates of “stress” (pitch, intensity, length). [...] Since “stress”, if existing, would be predictable from tone and tone needs to be marked underlyingly, we propose to cut out the middleman and analyze the requirement as weight-to-tone. Since toneless words are also stressless, this means that Lung’Ie has a culminative /H/ tone system that just happens to care about weight.
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: File checked: (+, UC eScholarship postprint of Probus 33(1), doi 10.1515/prbs-2021-0002). The three quoted stretches are present at the stated locators: (a) end of section 1, postprint pp. 2-3 ( lines 115-129): 'As will be seen, we conclude that Lung'Ie has a privative /H/ (high) tone system[fn 3] without stress, similar to other culminative H tone systems such as Somali (Hyman 1981, see also Green and Morrison 2016; Le Gac 2003), but with the unusual stress-like property of weight-to-tone.' -- only difference is a footnote callout '3' between 'system' and 'without'; (b) section 4.1 Nouns, postprint pp. 12-13 ( lines 538-545): 'The H can be in any syllable, although there is some skewing be…
new_statements.rule_in_words: No word stress. Word prominence is a single lexical (culminative, at most one per word, not obligatory) H tone whose position is unpredictable and stored per word; it usually sits on the syllable that carried stress in the Portuguese etymon (nouns with H: 68% penult, 23% final, 9% antepenult), and a heavy syllable (CVV/CVC, at most one per word) must carry it (weight-to-tone). Verbs and most African-origin nouns (and ideophones) are toneless and show no prominent syllable at all. The authors explicitly tested for and rejected metrical stress (no vowel-inventory asymmetry, no consonant strengthening, no clash resolution, no post-tonic effects).
new_statements.secondary_stress: None; no secondary prominence discussed (only one H per word; all other syllables toneless).
new_statements.exceptions: Five H-Ø verbs (víka, dáka, pɔ́di, méNdu, fɛ́di); 2 of 35 closed-syllable H-nouns and 4 of 49 long-vowel H-nouns with H off the heavy syllable; five all-Ø nouns with a closed syllable; monosyllabic nouns must bear H; recent Portuguese loans keep liquids in clusters/codas. Earlier analyses differ: Günther 1973 (tone H/L/R), Traill & Ferraz 1981 (free pitch accent, obligatory single prominence, position mostly = Portuguese stress), Maurer 2009 (two tones H/L; L-L words said to have final stress), Agostinho 2015/2019 (free lexical stress plus tone; new verbs default to final stress).
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level lexical prosody based on 517 items recorded in isolation and in 18 syntactic frames with five speakers (2019 fieldwork); phrase-level processes (final H deletion, contour flattening before pause, final-vowel devoicing) treated separately in §4.1.
new_statements.identity_note: All sources describe the same variety, Principense = Lung'Ie (prin1242, ISO pre), spoken on Príncipe; Agostinho & Hyman's data are from five elderly speakers recorded in 2019, Traill & Ferraz's from Ferraz's 1969/70 recordings. Not to be confused with Principense Portuguese (the local Portuguese variety studied in Wu & Agostinho 2026 etc.).

new_statements.quote: [p. 87] Por estes motivos, consideramos o lung’Ie como uma língua de padrão acentual misto, em que o acento é a principal categoria suprassegmental. [p. 92, 3.3.2] O lung’Ie possui um sistema de acento lexical livre, ou seja, cada palavra possui um acento idiossincrático e não é possível estabelecer uma regra fonológica para a atribuição deste acento na sílaba tônica original. [...] No caso dos verbos, o acento default é oxítono para palavras novas. [p. 93] O acento pode ser atribuído à última, penúltima ou antepenúltima sílaba. Apesar disso, como argumentado acima, não é possível estabelecer uma análise métrica que dê conta de prever o locus do acento em lung’Ie.
new_statements.translation: [p. 87] For these reasons we consider Lung'Ie a language with a mixed accentual pattern, in which stress is the main suprasegmental category. [p. 92] Lung'Ie has a free lexical stress system, i.e. each word has an idiosyncratic stress and it is not possible to establish a phonological rule assigning this stress to the original tonic syllable. [...] For verbs, the default stress is final (oxytone) for new words. [p. 93] Stress may be assigned to the final, penultimate or antepenultimate syllable. Nevertheless, as argued above, it is not possible to set up a metrical analysis that predicts the locus of stress in Lung'Ie.

new_statements.relation_note: The catalog record (world-2026-09-17) has an empty rule; the one existing statement (Agostinho & Hyman 2021, Probus) reads Lung'Ie as a privative /H/ tone system WITHOUT word stress. This 2015 thesis by the same first author states the opposite type: a free (lexical) contrastive stress system on one of the last three syllables, with tone secondary and largely predictable from stress ('mixed' system, stress the main suprasegmental category), plus predictable alternating secondary stress. The two agree on the locus facts (the prominent syllable — 'stressed' in 2015, H-toned/heavy in 2021 — is lexically specified within the last three syllables and verbs are prominence-final); they differ on w…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress is lexical (free), falling on one of the last three syllables (final, penult or antepenult) with no metrical rule; it is contrastive (minimal pairs such as [ˈkanɪ] 'carne' vs [kaˈni] 'inclinar a cabeça', [ˈkabɐ] 'cabra' vs [kaˈba] 'acabar'). Verbs are overwhelmingly final-stressed (default oxytone for new verbs; only four penult-stressed verbs: daka, fɛdɪ, mɛ̃dʊ, vika; past participles in -du always penult). The author treats Lung'Ie as a mixed stress-plus-tone system in which stress is the principal suprasegmental category: tone (Maurer's H/L patterns) is fully predictable from stress in verbs and partly in nouns (a stressed syllable never bears L if the word has any H; in disyllables stress falls on the leftmost H, else final), no phonological process refers to tone while apocope, diphthongization, nasalization, final raising and vowel sandhi refer to stress, and younger speakers retain only the stress system.
new_statements.secondary_stress: 3.3.3, p. 94: 'O acento secundário em lung’Ie ocorre em palavras com três sílabas ou mais e é previsível a partir do acento primário. Como o acento primário é à direita, o acento secundário cairá sobre a segunda sílaba à sua esquerda.' — secondary stress in words of three or more syllables, on the second syllable to the left of the primary (alternating), e.g. [taˌmutaˈmu], [ˌpiriˈkitʊ] 'periquito', [ˌpigiˈsɔzɔ] 'preguiçoso'.
new_statements.exceptions: Stress cannot fall on a syllable whose nucleus is a syllabic nasal; recent Portuguese loans keep Portuguese stress, so no default locus can be established for nouns; some trisyllabic nouns with all-L or all-H tone patterns (mutɐ̃bu 'armadilha', ukũdu, ukjabu 'quiabo', oroko, usuda) show variable penult~final stress depending on sentence position (focus), but the language game shows them to be underlyingly final-stressed; CVV words like [baː], [biː] are analysed as stressed monosyllables; three tonal minimal pairs (másu/másù, lɛta/lɛ̀ta, ùsã/ùsà̃) are not explained by stress and many speakers do not perceive them; the author flags that tone notations in the literature (Günther 1973, Ferraz & Traill 1981, Maurer 2009) disagree and that a deeper study of the stress-tone interaction is needed.
new_statements.identity_note: Both the thesis and the 2021 paper describe Lung'Ie as spoken on Príncipe Island (fieldwork 2009-2014 for the thesis, 2019 for the paper); the thesis notes (p. 87, p. 418) that younger speakers retain only the stress system, i.e. the tonal contrasts are reported mainly for older fluent speakers.

readall_conflicts: The only listed work could not be opened, so nothing new was read; the catalog's existing statement (Agostinho & Hyman 2021: privative /H/ tone system without stress, with weight-to-tone) stands as the reading of record. A real conflict in the literature is already visible from the works held by the project: Agostinho & Hyman 2021 (postprint p. 2) list four competing analyses of Lung'Ie word prosody, 'a fully-specified tone language with H, L and R tones (Günther 1973); a free "pitch accent" language with obligatory H (Traill and Ferraz 1981); a fully-specified tone language with H and L tones (Maurer 2009) and a mixed system of stress and tone (Agostinho 2015, 2016)', and then argue for privative H tone with no stress. The unopened 2015 thesis, per Agostinho 2019 (p. 79), posits lexically idiosyncratic (unpredictable) primary stress alongside tone, with final default stress for new verbs, and Maurer 2009: 27 posits final prominence in toneless words; Agostinho & Hyman 2021 (p. 30) explicitly reject that final-prominence claim. So the author's own 2015 position (lexical stress + tone) is superseded by her 2021 co-authored analysis (tone only, no stress), which is what the catalog records. The sources disagree on the TYPE of word prosody, not on where prominence sits. sources.note: Concludes Lung'Ie has a privative culminative but non-obligatory /H/ tone system 'without stress'; H position is lexical (any syllable; in H-nouns 68% penult, 23% final, 9% antepenult, reflecting Portuguese etymological stress via stress-to-tone), heavy syllables (CVV/CVC, max one per word) must carry the H ('weight-to-tone'); verbs and ~92% of African-origin nouns are toneless and show no prominent syllable; explicit search for stress correlates (vowel reduction, consonant strength, clash, post-tonic effects) found none. Notes Maurer 2009 'briefly mentions that L-L words have final stress'.

sources.citation: Traill, Anthony & Luiz Ferraz. 1981. The interpretation of tone in Principense Creole. Studies in African Linguistics 12(2): 205-215.
sources.note: Rejects Günther's tone-language analysis; proposes a 'free pitch accent' system: exactly one prominent syllable per word (H, Rise or Fall; all others L by accent reduction), any syllable may bear it; prominence usually falls where Portuguese had stress but not always (peru H-L < pe'ru, gira L-H < ga'linha, nuve L-H < 'nuvem); prominence = pitch with optional loudness/length.
